L374: Let S be a finite idempotent semigroup with central idempotents. This means that \(S^{2}=S\) and \(ea=ae\) for every \(a\in S\) and \(e\in E(S)\). Setting \(E=E(S)\), it is shown in [cite39†30 , Section 6] that every \(s\in S\) has a left (right) identity from E. If \(e,f\in E\) are right identities of a then ef is also an idempotent and a right identity of a. Since \(ef\le e,f\) we deduce that every \(a\in S\) has a minimum right identity.
L375: Since E is central it is clear that \(ef=e\iff fe=e\) and \(e\in E\) is a right identity of s if and only if it is left identity of s. Therefore, S is a reduced E-Fountain semigroup with \(s^{+}=s^{*}\) for every \(s\in S\).

L382: 
L383: $$ ba(ba^{*})^{*}=ba^{*}a(ba^{*})^{*}=ba^{*}(ba^{*})^{*}a=ba^{*}a=ba $$
L384:

L403: ## 5 Additional examples
L404: ### 5.1 The monoid of order-preserving functions
L405: Let \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {T}}\,}}_{n}\) be the monoid of all functions \(f:[n]\rightarrow [n]\) (where \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\)). A function \(f\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {T}}\,}}_{n}\) is called order-preserving if \(i\le j\implies f(i)\le f(j)\) for every \(i,j\in [n]\). We denote by \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) the submonoid of \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {T}}\,}}_{n}\) of all order-preserving functions.
L406: In this section we will see that \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) is a reduced E-Fountain semigroup that satisfies the generalized left ample condition so by the dual of Theorem cite60†3.12 there is an isomorphism \(\Bbbk {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\simeq \Bbbk _{0}\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) of \(\Bbbk \)-algebras for any commutative unital ring \(\Bbbk \). We will also describe more explicitly the composition in \(\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\).
L407: Elementary observations
L408: 
L409: Recall that the kernel of of a function \(f\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) — \(\ker (f)\) — is the equivalence relation on its domain defined by \((i_{1},i_{2})\in \ker (f)\) if and only if \(f(i_{1})=f(i_{2})\). Since f is order-preserving, the kernel classes of f are intervals — if \(i_{1}\le i_{2}\le i_{3}\) and \((i_{1},i_{3})\in \ker (f)\) then \((i_{1},i_{2})\in \ker f\) also.
L410: Let \(K_{1},\ldots ,K_{l}\) be the kernel classes of f. Let \(y_{i}=f(K_{i}\)) and assume that the indices are arranged such that \(y_{1}<y_{2}<\cdots <y_{l}\). Choose \(x_{i}\) to be the maximal element of \(K_{i}\) and note that it must be the case that \(x_{l}=n\). Now, set
L411: 
L412: $$ X=\{x_{1},\ldots ,x_{l}\},\quad Y=\{y_{1},\ldots ,y_{l}\} $$
L413: so from every \(f\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) we can extract two sets \(X,Y\subseteq [n]\) such that \(|X|=|Y|\) and \(n\in X\). In the other direction, from two such sets \(X=\{x_{1},\ldots ,x_{l}\}\) where \(x_{l}=n\) and \({Y=\{y_{1},\ldots ,y_{l}\}}\) we can retrieve an f by setting
L414: 
L415: $$ f(x)={\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} y_{1} & x\le x_{1}\\ y_{i} & x_{i-1}<x\le x_{i}\quad (2\le i\le l). \end{array}\right. } $$
L416: As a conclusion, we observe that there is a one-to-one correspondence between functions \(f\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) and pairs of sets \(X,Y\subseteq [n]\) such that \(|X|=|Y|\) and \(n\in X\). From now on we denote by \(f_{Y,X}\) the function associated with \(X,Y\subseteq [n]\) (in contrary to [cite42†27 , Section 4.2] where this function was denoted \(f_{X,Y})\).
L417: Note that \({{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(f_{Y,X})=Y\) (where \({{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(f)\) is the image of f) and X contains the maximal elements of the kernel classes of \(f_{Y,X}\). Another easy observation is that \(f_{Z,Y}f_{Y,X}=f_{Z,X}\).
L418: The monoid \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) is a regular submonoid of \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {T}}\,}}_{n}\) and its Green’s equivalence relations are well-known (see [cite65†6 , Section 2]). In particular:
L419: $$\begin{aligned} f_{Y_{1},X_{1}}\,{{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {L}}\,}}\,f_{Y_{2},X_{2}}&\iff \ker (f_{Y_{1},X_{1}})=\ker (f_{Y_{2},X_{2}})\iff X_{1}=X_{2}\\ f_{Y_{1},X_{1}}\,{{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {R}}\,}}\,f_{Y_{2},X_{2}}&\iff {{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(f_{Y_{1},X_{1}})={{\,\mathrm{\textsf{im}}\,}}(f_{Y_{2},X_{2}})\iff Y_{1}=Y_{2} \end{aligned}$$
L420: We want to define our distinguished set of idempotents E. Note that for every \(X\subseteq [n]\) with \(n\in X\) the function \(f_{X,X}\) is an idempotent that can be described by \(f_{X,X}(i)=\min \{x\in X\mid i\le x\}\). It will be convenient to define \(e_{X}=f_{X,X}\) where \(X\subseteq [n]\) with \(n\in X\) and we set \(E=\{e_{X}\mid n\in X\}\) (this is precisely the set of idempotents of the Catalan monoid — see [cite26†29 , Section 17.5.2]).

L615: In (cite17†Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk, 2011 , Theorem 1(viii)), it is shown that, in this case, $\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}$ is isomorphic to the Catalan monoid $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$. The Catalan monoid $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$ is the monoid of all order-preserving and order-decreasing total transformations of the set $[n+1]$. That is, the set of all $f:[n+1]\to[n+1]$ such that:
L616: 
L617:   1. (i)
L618: 
L619: $f(i)\leq f(j)$ for $i,j\in[n+1]$ with $i\leq j$ (order-preserving);
L620: 
L621:   2. (ii)
L622: 
L623: $f(i)\leq i$ for $i\in[n+1]$ (order-decreasing).
L624: The operation in $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$ is the usual composition and the unit element is the identity on $[n+1]$. For $f,g\in\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$, we denote by $fg=f\circ g$.
L625: 
L626: Catalan monoids and their presentations were studied in cite57†Solomon (1996) . In (cite58†Stanley, 1999 , 6.25(g)), it was shown that $|\mathcal{C}_{n+1}|=C_{n+1}$, where $C_{n}=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ denotes the $n$-th Catalan number.
L627: In the proof of (cite17†Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk, 2011 , Theorem 1(vii)), the authors use the fact that the transformations $T_{i}$ for $i=1,2,\dots,n$, defined by
L628: 
L629:  | $$T_{i}(j)=\begin{cases}i,&j=i+1,\\
L630: j,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}$$  |
L631: 
L632: generate $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$. The corresponding isomorphism of monoids from $\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}$ to $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$ is then given by the unique extension of the mapping $x_{i}\mapsto T_{i}$ and we denote it by $\tau$.

L635: Since $\Theta$ is acyclic, we have $A_{\Theta}=\mathbbm{2}^{[n]}$. For nonempty $X=\{i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k}\}\subseteq[n]$ with $i_{1}>i_{2}>\dots>i_{k}$, we have that $i_{j}\to i_{j^{\prime}}$ implies $j>j^{\prime}$. By Lemma cite38†2.7 , we have
L636: 
L637:  | $$e_{X}=x_{i_{k}}\dots x_{i_{2}}x_{i_{1}}.$$  |  | (4)
L638: Hence, in this case, idempotents are written as products in which the indices of the generators increase from left to right. Observe that in the Kiselman monoid, we have the converse case. We also denote $T_{X}=\tau(e_{X})$. In particular, $T_{\emptyset}$ is the identity on $[n+1]$.
L639: Since $\tau$ is an isomorphism of monoids, $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent in $\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}$ if and only if $T_{X}T_{Y}$ is an idempotent in $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$ and $e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}$ if and only if $T_{X}T_{Y}=T_{X\cup Y}$. By (cite49†3 ), we then have

L657: 
L658: Let $X\subseteq[n]$. Then we have

L144: ### 2.3 Idempotents in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$
L145: 
L146: For $X\subseteq V_{\Theta}$, denote by $\Theta[X]$ the full subgraph of $\Theta$ with vertex set $X$, that is, $\Theta[X]$ is an oriented graph with vertex set $X$ and for $x_{i},x_{j}\in X$, there is an arrow from $x_{i}$ to $x_{j}$ in $\Theta[X]$ if and only if there is an arrow from $x_{i}$ to $x_{j}$ in $\Theta$.
L147: 
L148: In (cite23†Forsberg, 2017 , Theorem 3.6), the following theorem is proved for a general finite simple oriented graph $\Theta$.
L149: ###### Theorem 2.5.
L150: 
L151: There is a bijection between idempotents in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$ and full subgraphs of $\Theta$ which do not contain any oriented cycles.
L152: 
L153: In the proof, an idempotent is mapped to the full subgraph of $\Theta$ whose vertex set is the content of the idempotent. Therefore, for each $X\subseteq V_{\Theta}$ such that $\Theta[X]$ does not contain any oriented cycles, there exists exactly one idempotent in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$ with content $X$. We denote this idempotent by $e_{X}$.
L154: We denote the following set
L155: 
L156:  | $$\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}=\{X\subseteq V_{\Theta}\mid\Theta[X]\text{ does not contain any oriented cycles}\}.$$  |
L157: ###### Remark 2.6.
L158: 
L159: If $Y\subseteq X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$, then $\Theta[Y]$ is a subgraph of $\Theta[X]$, and hence it does not contain any oriented cycles. Therefore, $Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$.
L160: 
L161: Theorem cite37†2.5 implies the following proposition.
L162: 
L163: ###### Proposition 2.7.
L164: 
L165: The set
L166: 
L167:  | $$\{e_{X}\mid X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}\}$$  |
L168: 
L169: is the set of all idempotents in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$.
L170: ###### Proposition 2.8.
L171: 
L172: Let $X,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$. Then $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$ if and only if $X\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$ and $e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}$.
L173: ###### Proof.
L174: 
L175: If $X\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$ and $e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}$, then $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent by Proposition cite38†2.7 . Conversely, if $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent, then by Proposition cite38†2.7 , there exists $Z\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$ such that
L176: 
L177:  | $$e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{Z}.$$  |
L178: 
L179: Taking contents, we get
L180: 
L181:  | $$Z=c(e_{Z})=c(e_{X}e_{Y})=c(e_{X})\cup c(e_{Y})=X\cup Y.$$  |
L182: 
L183: Hence $X\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$ and $e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}$. ∎
L184: The idempotent $e_{X}$ can be written explicitly. Note that if $\Theta[X]$ does not contain any oriented cycles, then we can write $X$ as $X=\{x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\}$ such that $x_{i_{j}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{j^{\prime}}}$ implies $j<j^{\prime}$ for all $j,j^{\prime}\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}$.
L185: ###### Lemma 2.9.
L186: 
L187: Let $X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$. Then for any ordering of the set $X=\{x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\}$ such that $x_{i_{j}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{j^{\prime}}}$ implies $j<j^{\prime}$ for all $j,j^{\prime}\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}$, we have
L188: 
L189:  | $$e_{X}=x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\dots x_{i_{k}}.$$  |
L190: 
L191: Moreover, we have $e_{X}z=ze_{X}=e_{X}$ for any $z\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$ with $c(z)\subseteq X$.
L192: ###### Proof.
L193: 
L194: Denote by
L195: 
L196:  | $$y=x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\dots x_{i_{k}}.$$  |
L197: 
L198: If $x_{i_{j}}\in X$, then
L199: 
L200:  | $$x_{i_{j+1}}x_{i_{j+2}}\dots x_{i_{k}}$$  |
L201: 
L202: is obtained by multiplying letters that do not admit arrows to $x_{i_{j}}$. Lemma cite36†2.2 implies
L203: 
L204:  | $$yx_{i_{j}}=x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{j-1}}(x_{i_{j}}x_{i_{j+1}}\dots x_{i_{k}}x_{i_{j}})=x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{j-1}}(x_{i_{j}}x_{i_{j+1}}\dots x_{i_{k}})=y.$$  |
L205: 
L206: By induction, we get
L207: 
L208:  | $$yx_{l_{1}}x_{l_{2}}\dots x_{l_{m}}=y,$$  |
L209: for any $x_{l_{1}},x_{l_{2}},\dots,x_{l_{m}}\in X$. This proves $yz=y$ for any $z\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$ with $c(z)\subseteq X$.
L210: 
L211: For any $x_{i_{j}}\in X$,
L212: 
L213:  | $$x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\dots x_{i_{j-1}}$$  |
L214: 
L215: is obtained by multiplying letters that do not admit arrows from $x_{i_{j}}$. Lemma cite36†2.2 implies
L216: 
L217:  | $$x_{i_{j}}y=(x_{i_{j}}x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{j-1}}x_{i_{j}})x_{i_{j+1}}\dots x_{i_{k}}=(x_{i_{1}}\dots x_{i_{j-1}}x_{i_{j}})x_{i_{j+1}}\dots x_{i_{k}}=y.$$  |
L218: 
L219: By induction, we again obtain
L220:  | $$x_{l_{1}}x_{l_{2}}\dots x_{l_{m}}y=y,$$  |
L221: 
L222: for any $x_{l_{1}},x_{l_{2}},\dots,x_{l_{m}}\in X$, which proves $zy=y$ for any $z\in\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$ with $c(z)\subseteq X$. Since $c(y)=X$, we have

L226: Hence $y$ is an idempotent in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$. Since $c(y)=X$, it follows that $y=e_{X}$. ∎
L227: ###### Definition 2.10.
L228: 
L229: A word $w\in F(V_{\Theta})$ is said to have no arrows from right to left if
L230: 
L231:  | $$w=x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\dots x_{i_{k}},$$  |
L232: 
L233: where $x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\in F(V_{\Theta})$ are letters, and if there is an arrow from $x_{i_{j}}$ to $x_{i_{j^{\prime}}}$ then $j<j^{\prime}$ for all $j,j^{\prime}\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}$.
L234: Moreover, for $X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$, $w$ is said to be $X$-topological if $w$ has no arrows from right to left, $c(w)=X$, and $\ell(w)=|X|$. In other words, $w$ is $X$-topological if there are no arrows from right to left and each letter $x_{i}$ with $x_{i}\in X$ occurs in $w$ exactly once.
L235: ###### Remark 2.11.
L236: 
L237: If $X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$, then $\Theta[X]$ is an acyclic oriented graph and hence there exists an $X$-topological word. Also observe that the empty word is $\emptyset$-topological.
L238: 
L239: ###### Lemma 2.12.
L240: 
L241: For $X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$, a word $w\in F(V_{\Theta})$ is $X$-topological if and only if $w$ is a normal form of $e_{X}$.
L242: ###### Proof.
L243: 
L244: If $w$ is $X$-topological, then $\pi(w)=e_{X}$ by Lemma cite39†2.9 . Moreover, since no letter in $w$ occurs more than once, no further elementary cancellations may be performed on $w$, and hence $w$ is a normal form of $e_{X}$.
L245: Now assume $w$ is a normal form of $e_{X}$. Since $X\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$, there exists an $X$-topological word $v$ by Remark cite40†2.11 . Hence, there are no arrows from right to left in $v$, $c(v)=X$, and $\ell(v)=|X|$. By the previous paragraph, $v$ is a normal form of $e_{X}$. By Theorem cite41†2.4 (cite42†i ), we have $w\sim v$. Since elementary commutations only interchange letters that are not connected, the relative order of any two letters that are connected by an arrow is preserved under $\sim$.
